activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Cortisol is a hormone made by the adrenal glands that rises during stress; when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high.
story:
The audition for the school storytelling guild was on Friday, and Emilia had been picked to try out, mostly because Brennan had stood up in class and said, "I nominate Emilia, because she tells the best endings." That had been two weeks ago. Since then her stomach hurt almost every morning, she could not fall asleep, and even her favourite cereal tasted like cardboard. Her mom noticed the dark circles under her eyes and made an appointment.

The doctor was brisk and kind. She listened, checked Emilia over, and said, "Nothing is broken. But your body has been running on cortisol. It's a hormone your adrenal glands make, and it rises during stress. When stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high, and that leaves you feeling run down." Emilia squinted at her. "So worry is a chemical?" The doctor shrugged. "It's one piece of it. The good news is that you can help your body lower it." On the drive home, Emilia turned the words over and over, like a stone in her pocket.

That evening she sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with a notebook and a plan. If worry raised this cortisol stuff, and if it hung around when stress went on and on, then maybe her stomach aches were not random. Maybe they were a pattern she could actually see. She drew a grid: seven columns for days, one row for "worry spike," one row for "stomach or sleep." Then she thought back to Saturday, when Archie had come over to practise stories in the garage.

She remembered it clearly. Archie had done his whole tale about the frozen lake twice, perfectly, and then said, "You go." Her hands had gone cold, her mind had gone blank, and she had mumbled something about homework and hidden in the bathroom for ten minutes. That night she had barely slept. She wrote it down: worry spike, Saturday afternoon; terrible sleep, Saturday night. Sunday she had relaxed, watching a movie with her dad, and she had slept fine. One data point each way. It fit.

"Archie," she said on Monday at lunch, "do you ever get scared before you perform?" He looked surprised. "Everyone does. Brennan says nobody's immune to nerves. He counts backwards from twenty and it works for him." Emilia nodded slowly. So the feeling was normal, even for Archie, even for Brennan. What mattered was what you did next. She tried the counting that afternoon in the garage, out loud, and Archie timed her with his watch. Her shoulders came down from around her ears.

By Thursday she had a new rule written in her notebook: spike the worry on purpose once a day, in small doses, then calm down on purpose, so her body could practise settling. She also told her mom she needed one boundary: no more surprise run-throughs at the dinner table, please, because being quizzed while eating made the spikes worse. Her mom agreed. On Friday morning her stomach was quiet. She stood in front of the guild, counted backwards in her head, and began, "Once there was a lake that froze in one night."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen every two hours outdoors, and immediately after swimming or sweating.
story:
The car was packed before sunrise, and Jordan bounced in his seat the whole drive to the coast. His dad had promised a full day at the beach, and Jordan had big plans: a sandcastle with a moat, a swim race with Abraham and Paxton, who were coming with their own families, and maybe, if the waves cooperated, his first attempt at bodyboarding. His mom slathered sunscreen on his shoulders in the parking lot while he squirmed and stared at the shimmering water.

The morning was everything he wanted. The dunes were lush with tall green grass, and the sand was already warm by nine. Jordan, Abraham, and Paxton dug a moat deep enough to flood at high tide, then charged into the waves for the swim race. Jordan won by half an arm. "Best vacation day ever," he announced, wringing out his shirt.

By late afternoon, though, his shoulders had turned an angry pink, and by dinner they stung so much he had to sit very still. That night he lay on the hotel bed, thinking hard. He'd had sunscreen on. He'd watched his mom put it on. So why the burn? He counted backward through the day. Sunscreen at nine. Swimming, sweating, more swimming, and nobody had touched the bottle again until it was too late. His dad, reading a memoir about a sailor crossing the Pacific, looked up and said, "Sunscreen wears off. That's just how it goes." Jordan frowned. He didn't think it just wore off on a schedule. Something about the water and the sweat seemed important, and he wanted to test it.

The next morning he declared a plan. "New rule," he told Abraham and Paxton as they spread towels near the lifeguard stand. "Sunscreen now, and then we do it again every two hours, and right after we swim. Not later. Right after." Paxton groaned, but Jordan set a timer on his watch and stood guard over the bottle like it was treasure.

They swam at eleven, and the moment Jordan's feet hit dry sand he was squirting white cream into his palms and chasing his friends down the beach. "Every two hours, and immediately after swimming or sweating," he repeated, dabbing Paxton's nose while Abraham laughed. At one o'clock the timer beeped and they lined up again without complaint, because by then even Paxton admitted it might be working. When the sun finally sank behind the dunes, Jordan checked his shoulders in the bathroom mirror. Not pink. Not even a little. He grinned at his reflection and pumped both fists in the air. "Same rule tomorrow," he called through the door. "And I call first bodyboard run."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A message sent in a private chat can be screenshotted and shared by anyone who receives it, so a private message is only as private as the people who read it.
story:
Nathaniel sat at the kitchen computer in his cargo shorts, clicking refresh for the third time, as if the group chat might change on its own. It didn't. The screenshot was still there, pinned by Eli: a private message Nathaniel had sent him two nights ago, the one that said Onyx's science presentation was "a slow-motion disaster." Below it, Onyx had typed a single question mark.

He heard his mom's voice from the hallway. "Ten more minutes, then you have to comply with the screen rule, mister." Normally he would have bargained. Now he just nodded, because his stomach was doing something like a laundry spin cycle.

He thought about how the message had traveled. He had sent it to one person, in a private chat, at ten at night. It had shown up in a group chat with eleven people in it by lunch the next day. He hadn't posted it there. Eli had. The message itself hadn't leaked out like water through a crack; it had been carried, whole and intact, by someone who had it. Nathaniel rubbed his chin. So a private message wasn't guarded by anything except the person on the other end. If that person shared it, it was public, and there was no taking it back.

He had a theory, and he wanted to test it before he lost his nerve. He opened the private chat with Eli and typed: "Did you screenshot it and put it in the group, or did somebody else?" Then he sat on his hands, literally, because otherwise they would keep typing.

The reply came fast. "i screenshotted it to show my cousin bc i thought it was funny. then he musta sent it to the group. im sorry man."

Nathaniel read it twice. Eli hadn't meant to blow anything up, but that hardly mattered now, because the message had still escaped, twice over. He took a breath and typed one more thing, a message he actually meant, not the fast joke from two nights ago. Then he walked to Onyx's house, three blocks away, because some things deserved to be said out loud with actual air between people.

Onyx opened the door with his arms crossed. "If you're here to say it was fake, forget it."

"I'm here because typing was easier than this, and that was the problem," Nathaniel said. "My apology is more authentic in person. Even if it's less convenient."

Onyx stared at him for a second, then snorted. "Less convenient. Yeah, I'll say." He stepped back from the door. "You want the last slice of pizza? It's only slightly a disaster."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
The arguments started at the very first practice. Finnegan wanted to take every free kick, Stanley kept shouting at the defenders, and Jake got knocked over twice because nobody passed to anyone. On the walk home, his mom handed him a folded note from the coach's mailbox, the one she'd agreed to deliver. "Your team is new," the coach had written. "Give it time. Skills grow in strange ways. P.S. There is a box of old books at the field shed if you're bored on rainy days."

Jake remembered the shed from last summer, when he and Stanley had hidden in it during a thunderstorm and counted thunder claps until the rain stopped. So after the next disaster of a practice, a game against the Grey Wolves that they lost four to nothing, he went looking. Behind the cones and the rolled-up nets sat a paperback with a cracked spine, and inside it he found a chapter about how groups develop. A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman had proposed, way back in 1965, that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing. Jake read the line three times. Storming. That was exactly his team.

He tested the idea instead of just believing it. At the next practice he counted arguments, quietly, in his head: Finnegan versus Stanley about positions, then Stanley versus the keeper about a dropped ball. Seven arguments in forty minutes. But he also noticed something the others missed, a pattern you couldn't see in any single moment. Each quarrel ended a little faster than the one before, and afterward the players sorted themselves out without being told. It was cumulative, small fixes stacking up, the way snow builds a drift one flake at a time. When a ball rolled into the hedge, Finnegan was the one who ran to extract it from the branches, even though he never did chores like that before.

Still, the biggest controversy was who would be captain. Finnegan wanted it so badly that he'd started wearing an old armband he found at home, and Stanley wanted it too, which was half the shouting. Jake didn't say a word about Tuckman to either of them. He just kept counting practices, watching the storming shrink.

By the fifth week the counting showed almost nothing. One small disagreement about whose throw-in it was, settled in ten seconds. When the Grey Wolves came for the rematch, the passing went sideways and backward, smooth as water finding its way downhill, and Jake scored the second goal in a three-one win.

After the whistle, Finnegan pulled the armband off and held it out. "You take it," he said. "You noticed everything before we did."

Jake slid it on over his sleeve.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Havdalah, a Hebrew word meaning separation, is the ceremony that ends Shabbat on Saturday night once three stars can be seen in the sky.
story:
Zoe had agreed to try her grandmother's day of rest for one Saturday, which meant no phone from sundown Friday until Saturday night. Her stomach growled all afternoon because she was fasting too, and by dinner she was staring out the window at a sky turning from orange to gray.

"When does this end?" she asked.

"When we see three stars," her grandmother said. "Then we say Havdalah. It's a Hebrew word. It means separation."

"Separation of what?"

Her grandmother only smiled and handed her a translucent blue scarf. "Put this over your eyes and look up. It softens the glare, so stars stand out better. My mother taught me that trick."

Zoe stepped onto the porch with her cousin, and the two of them began the old race in the family, the race to count the first three stars. Zoe held the scarf to her eyes and scanned. One star, then two, both low over the barn. Then clouds rolled in and covered everything. She waited. Her cousin went inside. The sky stayed solid gray, and she thought about the principle behind the whole day: the rest did not end because you were tired of it, it ended because of something outside yourself, something you could not hurry. She tested the idea by trying to spot stars through a thin patch, but nothing came through.

Inside, her grandmother had left the phone messages on the counter for her, since Zoe could not check them herself. There was one from Ellen, printed on paper in her grandmother's looping handwriting: "Zoe, my mom says your fast starts when? I want to try it with you next Saturday. Text me back after your stars. Three, right? Ellen."

Zoe had planned to quit after this one day. She read the note twice. Then she went back out to the porch, scarf in hand, and the clouds had thinned, and there, above the barn, a third star had appeared while she wasn't watching.

"Grandma!" she shouted through the screen door. "Three! I see three!"

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Snow squeaks underfoot when it is very cold, because the hard ice crystals rub and break instead of melting slightly under pressure.
story:
The phone buzzed at 6:40 and Riley read the word every kid hopes for: closed. Snow day. He was out the door by eight, boots on, because the park two blocks away had the only hill in the neighborhood worth sledding, and Jeremiah had already texted MEET AT THE TOP.

Halfway there he noticed something odd. Every step made a high squeak, like a rubber duck being stepped on. Squeak, squeak, squeak, all the way to the corner. On the last block before the park, though, the sound changed. Under the big bare tree the snow still squeaked, but where sunlight had been beating on a drift beside the fence, his boots went quiet, sinking in with a soft crunch and no squeak at all. He stopped, backed up, and stepped on the sunny patch again. Nothing. He stepped onto the shady sidewalk. Squeak.

Jeremiah was already dragging his sled up the hill. "Took you long enough."

"Listen to this," Riley said. He walked a slow circle. "It only squeaks in the shade. The sunny snow doesn't." Jeremiah tried it, stomping first on one side of the path and then the other, and frowned when his boots agreed.

Riley crouched and pressed his mitten into the sunny snow. It gave easily, and a little water darkened his glove. Then he pressed the same mitten into the shady snow and it stayed dry and hard, grains scraping against each other. He stood up slowly. "I think it squeaks when it's really cold, because the ice crystals are hard, and they rub and break instead of melting a little under your boot. In the sun the snow softens, so it just squishes." He decided to make sure. He took a census of the park in his head, counting places like a scientist counting birds: shady steps, squeaky; sunny bench drift, silent; the north side of the drinking fountain, squeaky again. Every cold spot sang, every warm one hushed. Seven to three.

"Great, mystery solved," Jeremiah said, already climbing. "Now watch this." He aimed his sled at a bump near the fence that most kids avoided. Riley called it reckless, and Jeremiah just grinned and pushed off. He caught air on the bump, flew, and rolled to a stop in a soft sunny drift, the one silent patch on the whole hill, laughing with snow down his collar.

They were brushing off the sled when Ms. Sun came through the gate with her dog. "You two are nurturing those lungs with this cold air," she said, and pulled a thermos from her bag. "Cocoa, if you help me find the dog's ball. It went somewhere in the squeaky part."

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: The official Monopoly rules say that if a player lands on an unowned property and chooses not to buy it, the bank auctions it to the players.
story:
Payton had been at Camp Birchwood for six days, and the rainy afternoon had driven her whole cabin into the mess hall, where Angus was setting up a battered Monopoly board with the confidence of a general. He claimed the top hat before anyone else could grab it. Raymond took the dog, which he said was versatile because it could be a pet, a guard, or a piece in a game, and Payton settled for the thimble.

The trouble started on Raymond's second trip around the board. He landed on Marvin Gardens, counted his money twice, and shook his head. "Not buying it. Too expensive." He set the dice down and waited for Angus to roll.

"You can't just skip it," Angus said.

"Watch me," said Raymond.

They argued while the rain hammered the windows. Angus said skipping let Raymond hoard his cash and wait for better properties. Raymond said it was his money and nobody could make him spend it. Payton, who had been quiet, started to wonder if the real problem was not Raymond's stubbornness but a missing rule. Maybe the game assumed something that they had all been doing wrong. She had a theory: the designers must have thought about this exact situation, and if so, there would be an answer in the folded paper tucked under the board, which nobody ever read.

She pulled it out and flattened it on the table. The print was tiny, so she traced each line with her finger until she found it. "Here. It says if a player lands on an unowned property and chooses not to buy it, the bank auctions it to the players."

"Auction?" Raymond leaned over the sheet.

"Selling it to whoever bids," Angus said. "Like on that show my grandma watches."

Payton grinned. "So we simulate an auction. The banker starts the bidding at, say, half the price, and we all bid, even you, Raymond. Whoever bids highest gets it. That's the fair rule, straight from the box, and it fixes the problem you made, which was hoarding cash while good properties sit there."

Raymond squinted at the rules sheet, then at Marvin Gardens, then at his pile of bills. "Fine. Start it at fifty dollars."

Angus opened the bidding. Raymond, who it turned out could not bear losing anything, even something he had refused moments earlier, ran the price up to a hundred and ten. "Sold," Payton announced, and slid him the deed.

"You just paid more than you would have," Angus said, delighted.

"He's like a herbivore that suddenly decides it wants the whole garden," Payton said, and Raymond laughed so hard he knocked the dog into theChance pile.

After that, every landed-on property went up for auction, and the game moved fast and loud and fair. Near supper time, Ms. Joseph paused by their table on her way to ring the bell. "I can hear you three from the craft room. What happened?"

Payton held up the rule sheet. "We found the rule nobody ever reads."

Ms. Joseph smiled and reached for the bell. "Then hurry up and finish. The herbivore still owns half the board."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855.
story:
Norah sat down at the last free computer in the lab and opened the class group chat. Forty-one unread messages, most of them in capital letters. "WHO ATE MY PROPELLER," someone had typed, meaning the little plastic spinner from the science shelf. It was Bilal's propeller, and Bilal typed everything in capitals, even "GOOD MORNING."

"That's the problem," Norah said. "We need actual rules. Ms. Ramírez said we could write them ourselves, but I don't want to just presume we're the first people who ever needed them. Somebody must have done this before."

Onyx leaned over from the next computer. "Online manners? People wrote books about that?"

"Not books. Look." Norah typed netiquette history into the search bar. The first real result made her stop. In 1995, a guide called "Netiquette Guidelines" was published, and it wasn't a book at all. It was a numbered document, RFC 1855, part of a series that engineers used to share technical rules.

"Netiquette Guidelines," Onyx read out loud. "That's really what it's called?"

"1995," Norah said. "Before we were born. Before our parents even had phones that did this." She skimmed the document. Some of it was about things she'd never heard of, but parts of it matched the chat exactly. Don't type in capitals, because it reads like shouting. Don't repeat what someone told you privately. Think about who can see what you send.

Onyx scrolled with her. "This part says a private message is different from a mailing list."

"So the chat is public," Norah said. "Everybody sees it. If you want to tell one person something, you message them directly." She thought about that. Last week she had posted in the chat that Bilal had failed the math quiz, because she thought it was funny. Bilal hadn't spoken to her much since. She had put something private into a public place.

She started a new document: Rules for Our Chat, in plain lowercase, with the credit at the bottom, Based on "Netiquette Guidelines", RFC 1855, 1995. Bilal walked in mid-lesson, read over her shoulder, and frowned.

"I don't shout," he said.

"It reads like shouting when everything's capitals," Norah said. "Even 'GOOD MORNING.'"

Bilal typed a test message in the chat, all lowercase, and the class stared at it like a rare bird. "Feels quiet," he said, and typed the next one normal again.

Then Ms. Ramírez came around and read the rules. "Good work. One question. Who reported that someone ate Bilal's propeller? I found it in the drawer where the thermometers go."

"Ate," Onyx said slowly. "Nobody ate it. It was just missing."

Norah went back through the chat. The drawer by the window, she remembered, was the one Bilal always knocked with his elbow when he squeezed past. She pulled it open. There, under the ruler, sat the propeller.

"Case closed," she said, and held it up. "One more rule: check the drawer before you accuse the class of eating anything."

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: In 2013 the US Federal Trade Commission told search engines that paid results must be clearly distinguishable from natural results, or they risk deceiving users.
story:
Violet's mother had a rule for take-your-daughter-to-work day: stay at the desk by the window, finish homework, and ask before touching the printer. Violet finished her homework by ten thirty and then opened the search bar on the spare laptop, because her class was having a debate on Friday and she was supposed to bring evidence.

The question Mr. Bakker had written on the board was simple. Is it fair for an advertisement to dress itself up as a search result? Sawyer had said yes, because companies pay for their spots and everybody knows how the web works. Pierre-Olivier had said no, because a kid looking for facts might click the paid thing and never find the real one. Violet had promised to find out what the actual rule was.

She typed her first keywords, "ads search results," and got a heap of pages about how to buy ads. Then she typed "are ads and search results different rules" and got an article about email spam. She leaned back. The problem wasn't the answers, it was the question. She tried "federal rule search engines paid results." The fourth result looked promising, from an official-looking site, so she clicked it.

Last summer, before school started, she had spent a whole afternoon trying to find a diagram of a volcano for a poster, and the top three links had all been trying to sell her a science kit. She remembered the abrupt jump from hope to annoyance when she realized none of them had the diagram at all. She had given up and drawn the volcano from a library book. This time she knew what to watch for.

On the new page she found what she needed. In 2013 the US Federal Trade Commission had told search engines that paid results must be clearly distinguishable from natural results, or they risk deceiving users. Violet read it twice, then opened her notebook and copied it down, word by word, because Mr. Bakker wanted sources. The page also used a word she wrote in the margin, "amendment," in a sentence about a change to some earlier guidance, and she looked it up quickly to be sure.

She scrolled back up and checked the top of the results page again. The first link had a small pale label that said "Ad" beside it. She had almost missed it. She decided to test the idea, so she ran three more searches and counted the labels. Two, one, and three ads sat at the top each time, each one marked, each one styled just enough like the others to insulate it from notice.

She printed her notes, asked first as required, and texted Sawyer from the desk phone by the window. "Found the rule. 2013. They have to mark them or it counts as deceiving users."

"Bring snacks Friday," Sawyer texted back.

fact: A minus sign placed directly before a word, with no space, removes results containing that word, so jaguar -car finds the animal instead of the car.
story:
Eve sat at the kitchen table with the family laptop open and a library book about rainforests next to her elbow. Her project on jaguars was due Friday, and every search she tried gave her pages and pages of car dealerships. The animal had somehow become one of the most notorious name-sharers on the internet.

Alicia leaned over her shoulder, holding her own stack of note cards. "I need the laptop after you. I'm doing my project on Rosa Parks, and I want to find her memoir, not a book report somebody wrote about it."

"Then stop reading over my shoulder and help me," Eve said. She typed jaguar facts again and counted the results. Nine of the first ten were about cars, with prices and lease offers. She tried jaguar animal and still got a dealership at the top, next to a box marked Ad. "That one's an ad. It says so in tiny letters." She scrolled past it. The real results underneath were still mostly cars.

She stared at the search box and thought about how the engine worked. Somewhere there was a rule, invisible, deciding what counted and what didn't. If there was a rule, she could test it. She tried jaguar NOT car, which she'd seen in the library catalog, but the results barely changed. Then she remembered the catalog help page differently and typed jaguar -car, the minus sign pressed right up against the word with no space. She hit enter. The dealerships vanished. Every result on the first page was the animal, and the second page too. "It works," she said. "The minus sign right before a word knocks out anything with that word in it. Watch, I'll diagnose it. Same search, space after the minus." She typed jaguar - car and the cars came flooding back. She deleted the space and they were gone again.

"Okay, that's actually useful," Alicia said, pulling the laptop toward her. "So I could search Rosa Parks memoir -report and skip the book reports." She typed it, and the first thing on the screen was the memoir itself, the real one, with her face on the cover. Eve slid her rainforest book across the table and said, "Copy that trick onto my note card before you hog the whole laptop."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Japanese uses different family words for your own family and someone else's: you call your own mother "haha" when talking to others, but a friend's mother is "okaasan."
story:
Jaxon had practiced his Japanese sentences all week, muttering them on the bus, in the shower, and once in his sleep, according to his sister. Now he stood at the cultural festival beside the paper lantern display, waiting his turn at the language booth, where anyone who spoke three full sentences about their family earned a folding fan. He wanted that fan more than he had wanted anything since the skating rink announced it would retire at the end of summer.

"Watch this," he whispered to Eileen, who was filming him for their class project.

A woman behind the booth smiled and gestured for him to begin. Jaxon took a breath. "Watashi no okaasan wa yasashii desu," he said proudly. My mother is kind. Then he added, "Watashi no haha wa ringo ga suki desu." My mother likes apples.

The woman blinked. So did the teenage volunteer beside her, who leaned over and murmured something Jaxon couldn't catch.

"What?" Jaxon asked Eileen. "Did I say apples wrong?"

Eileen rewound her video. "You said okaasan the first time and haha the second time. Two different words for mother."

Jaxon stared at the booth. Both words meant mother, but the woman had reacted exactly when he switched between them. There had to be a pattern. Maybe it was like the difference between "my dog" and "your dog," the way he wouldn't call Kesler's beagle by his own dog's name. He thought about the polite words his karate teacher used for other people's belongings. Then he had an idea, and it felt a little like lightning.

He turned back to the woman. "Okaasan is for someone else's mother," he said slowly, "and haha is for my own."

The woman's whole face brightened, luminous in the lantern light, and she clapped twice. "Hai! Correct!"

The teenage volunteer laughed. "You figured it out faster than most adults."

"Better than the time he called the tea vessel a soup bowl," Eileen said, deadpan.

Jaxon groaned, but he took his fan with both hands and bowed, deeply, the way his teacher had shown him, and the woman bowed right back.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Fresh fruits and vegetables are often cheapest at the peak of their local harvest season, when farmers have the most to sell.
story:
The gas station at the edge of town had one old cooler, humming away to regulate its temperature, and beside it a wooden shelf where a local farmer left pints of strawberries each morning. Brooklyn stood in front of that shelf with four crumpled dollars in her pocket. Four dollars was all she had, and she needed strawberries because her class was hosting a potluck of world cuisine on Friday, and she had promised to bring the strawberry shortcake her grandmother used to make.

Last month the pints had been four dollars each, and she had walked home empty-handed. Today a cardboard sign leaned against the shelf, and she read it twice to be sure. "Peak harvest, two dollars a pint." Behind the station she could see the farmer's truck parked in the shade, its bed stacked with crate after crate of berries, more crates than Brooklyn had ever seen there before. She turned to Iyad, who was counting quarters at the ice cream freezer. "Last month it was four dollars for this same pint," she said. "Do you think that's why it's cheaper now, because he has so many?"

Iyad pressed his face to the freezer glass. He wanted the rocket-shaped popsicle with the bubblegum eyes, but it cost two dollars and he only had six quarters. "Maybe," he said. "Test it. Ask him."

Brooklyn walked around to the truck. The farmer was rearranging crates, sliding the softest berries to the top so they would sell first. "Excuse me," Brooklyn said. "If I come back next week, will the pints still be two dollars?" The farmer wiped his hands on his jeans and looked at his truckload. "Probably less fruit by then," he said. "Depends what the fields give."

That was enough of an answer for her. She counted her crumpled dollars, bought two full pints, and carried them back inside with the red juice already staining her fingertips. At the freezer she held out one berry to Iyad, who had finally stacked his six quarters on the counter. "Tell you what," she said. "You split the popsicle, and I'll give you three strawberries for the shortcake topping."
