fact: Glossophobia is the name for fear of public speaking, and it is one of the most commonly reported fears.
story:
Kaitlyn had four notecards, a deadline of nine a.m. tomorrow, and an opening line about recycling that could put a room full of ten-year-olds to sleep. She knew the rules well enough by now. Mr. Doyle wanted a hook first, then three points, then a closing that circled back around. Her three points were fine. It was the hook that was the problem. She read it to the wall of the library, where she had retired to a corner table after school, and even the wall looked bored.

Eleanor and Adalyn found her there, spreading their own notecards like survivors comparing supplies. "Read yours out loud," Adalyn said, so Kaitlyn did, and her voice wobbled halfway through the second card. Her hands were shaking too. She stared at them, betrayed.

"Mine do that too," Eleanor said, holding out her own hands. They were steady as stones, which ruined the effect, but she added, "They did at lunch. When I was practicing."

Adalyn looked up from her cards. "There's a word for it, you know. My cousin told me. It's called glossophobia. Fear of public speaking. And it's one of the most commonly reported fears there is."

Kaitlyn turned this over. If the fear was that common, then half the room tomorrow would have shaking hands too, which meant everyone would be busy worrying about their own cards to notice hers. That was a hidden fact she couldn't see directly, but she could test it. She flipped her first notecard face down, retiring it for good, and wrote a new hook on the back. Then she tried it out, right there at the library table, with her two friends as the audience.

"Raise your hand if you'd rather do extra math homework than stand up here," she began. Adalyn raised both hands. Eleanor raised one and a pencil.

The next morning Mr. Doyle called names in order, and Kaitlyn was third. Walking up, she noticed the boy ahead of her pressing his cards flat against his leg, and the girl after him staring at the floor like it might open and save her. Commonly reported, indeed. She set her cards down, took a breath, and let her hook steer the room like a rudder, quietly and in one direction.

"Raise your hand if you'd rather do extra math homework," she said, "than stand up here." Every hand went up, including Mr. Doyle's.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: A top, or apex, predator is at the end of its food chain and, as an adult, has no natural predators of its own.
story:
Mathis crouched between the tomato rows with his notebook balanced on his knee, trying to draw arrows in the right order. Sun, then plants, then something that ate the plants, then something that ate that. The assignment was due Monday, and Ms. Munro had said the drawing had to end with the top of the chain, whatever that meant. Heat radiated from the black soil and made his pencil sweaty in his grip.

Gianluca and Oskar arrived on their bikes, arguing before they even dropped their kickstands. "It's an owl," Oskar said. "Owls hunt at night and nothing messes with them." "A hawk," Gianluca insisted. "In our woods the hawk is the top. I saw one take a squirrel right off the fence." They both looked at Mathis, who was the one actually doing the assignment.

Mathis thought about it while he sketched. A hawk ate snakes, and snakes ate grasshoppers, and grasshoppers ate the bean leaves that grew because of the sun. He tested the idea out loud, counting on his pencil. "Nothing eats the hawk, though. Nothing eats the owl either. Grown ones." Oskar frowned. "So they're both at the top?" Mathis drew a small arrow back from the hawk to the soil. "The top predator is the end of its chain, and when it's an adult, nothing hunts it. My mom said that's called an apex predator." Gianluca looked almost disappointed. "So our argument was useless?" "Both right," Mathis said. "In a vain kind of way."

Ms. Munro came over with a watering can and peered at his page. "Good, but you're missing the second half. What happens if one link disappears?" She pointed at a row of bean plants that had been stripped to skeletons. "Something's been at those. Whole link gone." She sighed and mentioned that half the gardeners had almost quit last spring when the city wanted to sell the land to a developer, and everyone still paying a mortgage on their houses couldn't afford plot fees too. "One link," she said, and walked on.

Mathis stared at the stripped plants. If the grasshoppers ate every leaf, the plants made no beans. Then whatever ate the beans went hungry, and the snakes got thin, and the hawk at the end of the chain felt it too, even though it lived far above the garden and nothing dared hunt it. He began drawing it as a chain with one glowing link going dark, arrows fading out above it.

"Draw the hawk twice," Oskar said, leaning over his shoulder. "Once at the top, and once at the empty end." Mathis grinned and pressed his pencil down. "Pass me the green one. This thing needs to look like something died in the middle of it."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language', published in 1755, helped settle how many English words were spelled.
story:
Gavin had spent his whole lunch break in the community center library, and now the spelling bee started in ten minutes. He hadn't meant to get distracted, but a fat old book with a cracked leather cover had caught his eye. Its title page said A Dictionary of the English Language, and below the name it said Samuel Johnson, 1755.

"Who decided how words are spelled?" Gavin asked, turning the yellowed pages. "Somebody had to pick."

Sami leaned over from the next chair. "My brother says spellings just, like, happened. Nobody picked anything."

Gavin ran his finger down a column of words. "Somebody printed this whole book, though. That's deciding." He wondered how much power a single dictionary could have, whether every speller after that had followed one man's choices. He couldn't see the answer, so he decided to test a simple idea: he would find the librarian and ask.

The librarian, stacking returns behind the desk, smiled at his question. "Samuel Johnson's A Dictionary of the English Language, published in 1755, helped settle how many English words were spelled," she said. "People copied dictionaries. They still do."

"So when I spell a word right," Gavin said slowly, "I'm agreeing with him."

"Sort of," she said, and turned back to her cart.

In the gym, folding chairs squeaked and Ms. Chan checked the microphone. Brent sat two seats over, bouncing his knee. "I've been impulsive all week," he whispered. "I didn't study, I just guessed at flash cards."

"You should have illustrated your words," Gavin said. "Draw them. My mom says pictures stick."

The first rounds went fast. Brent went out on "rhythm" and shrugged, not too upset. Then Ms. Chan said, "Gavin. Larva."

The word felt old, like something Johnson might have printed himself. Gavin thought of the fat book, of one man choosing letters that everyone after would copy. L-A-R-V-A.

The judges nodded, and Ms. Chan smiled and said, "Correct."

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Overmixing muffin batter develops gluten in the flour, which makes muffins tough and can leave long tunnels inside them.
story:
The camp stove had only one burner, but the old oven in the shelter worked, so Mathis set the dial to preheat and laid out the recipe card on the picnic table. Sophie had bet him a whole bag of marshmallows that he could not bake muffins from start to finish, and he intended to thwart her plan to win. "Four hundred degrees," he read aloud. "It has to be hot before the batter goes in."

He measured the flour, the sugar, the baking powder, then cracked the eggs into the bowl. He remembered last summer at his grandmother's, when he had watched her stir muffin batter exactly twelve times and stop, even though the batter still looked lumpy. He had thought that was naive, like she had just lost count. "It's gluten," she had said back then, tapping the spoon. "Too much stirring and it makes them tough." Now he dumped the wet ingredients into the dry ones and began to stir, and stir, and stir some more, until every lump vanished and the batter sat smooth as pudding.

The muffins rose beautifully. That was the frustrating part. They looked golden and perfect, and Mathis carried the tin to the table where Sophie and Landon were waiting with plates. Then he bit into one and stopped. It was chewy, almost rubbery, nothing like his grandmother's. He pulled one apart and stared. Long tunnels ran through the inside like wormholes in dirt. "That's weird," Landon said, leaning over. "Mine never look like that at home."

Mathis set his muffin down and thought. His grandmother's batter had been lumpy. His was smooth. Same flour, same oven, same recipe, different insides. The only thing he had changed was the stirring. He turned the muffin half over in his hand, following one tunnel from top to bottom, and the pieces came together. "I stirred it too much," he said slowly. "The gluten thing she told me about. Smooth batter, tough muffins."

"Try again tomorrow," Sophie said, already reaching for the butter. "And this time stop when it's ugly." Mathis copied the recipe onto a fresh card and wrote one rule across the top in capital letters: STOP AT LUMPY. He propped it against the sugar bag where he would see it first thing. "Twelve stirs," he said. "Count them."

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: The phrase "according to Hoyle" means following the rules exactly; it comes from Edmond Hoyle, whose 1742 book set down the rules of the card game whist.
story:
Payton set the deck of cards in the middle of the dinner table while her mother cleared the plates. Henley had stayed for lasagna, and now the two of them were three rounds into a game of Whist, which Payton's grandfather had promised to teach them after dinner. The trouble started immediately.

"You led with a heart," Henley said. "You can't do that."

"I can if I don't have any spades," Payton said. "That's just how it works."

"That's how it works in YOUR head." Henley's voice climbed. "You keep changing it so you win."

Payton felt something hot building in her chest, and she recognized it as resentment, the same feeling that had ruined their checkers tournament last month. She took a breath. "Okay. Wait. The problem isn't the heart. The problem is we never agreed on the rules in the first place. So let's name one rule we both think is fair and stick to it."

"Fine," Henley said. "If you don't have the suit that was led, you can play anything."

"Deal."

Her grandfather, who had been watching from the head of the table, tapped the deck. "Now you're playing according to Hoyle."

"Who's Hoyle?" Payton asked. "One of your old card friends?"

He chuckled. "My card club is nearly extinct, but Hoyle is older than all of us. Edmond Hoyle wrote a book in 1742 that set down the rules of whist. 'According to Hoyle' means following the rules exactly."

Payton picked up her phone and photographed the little rule card he kept in the card box, then texted the picture to Henley so the phone could transmit it to her too. "Now we both have the same rules," she said. "No arguing over what's in whose head."

Henley looked at the picture, then at her hand of cards, and laid down the queen of hearts without a single complaint. "Your lead," she said.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: During puberty the larynx, or voice box, grows larger and the vocal cords get longer and thicker, which makes the voice deeper, especially in boys.
story:
The waiting room of the dentist's office smelled like mint, and Landon was reading a poster about how bees pollinate apple trees when his voice broke. He had been telling Aron about the new soccer tryouts, something like "and then the coach said I could play forward," and halfway through "forward" his voice dropped like a stone down a well, then squeaked back up. Aron nearly fell off his chair laughing.

"It wasn't that funny," Landon said, except it came out in two different pitches, which made it funnier.

"It was significant," Aron wheezed. "It was the most significant thing I've heard all week."

At the front desk, Makai was waiting too, because their whole class had fluoride appointments on the same afternoon. "My brother's voice does that," Makai said. "It means you're growing. My mom made my brother start showering every single day and using deodorant, because growing makes you smell like a locker room."

"That's not a thing," Landon said, but he sniffed his own sleeve anyway, quietly.

He thought about it in the chair, while the hygienist scraped his teeth. Aron's brother was fifteen and his voice was deep as a tuba. Landon's cousin was thirteen and squeaked constantly. It was a pattern, like the bees on the poster: same cause, same result, over and over. He couldn't see the cause directly, but he could test it. On the way out, he stopped at the display rack by the cashier and read the little booklet called Your Changing Body. There it was, in the section on the larynx. "The larynx," he read aloud, careful not to crack, "is the voice box."

Aron leaned over his shoulder. "So?"

"So during puberty the larynx grows bigger, and the vocal cords get longer and thicker, and that makes your voice deeper. Especially in boys." Landon held up the booklet like a trophy. "That's why it cracks. It's growing, like my feet."

"Put it back, it costs money," Makai said, but the cashier waved them off.

"My mom's already buying me deodorant," Aron said as they pushed through the door into the sunshine. "At great expense, according to her. And the shower thing is a rule now."

"Mine too, starting tonight," Landon declared, and on the walk home he told them the whole tuba plan, and his voice only broke twice.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be false; 'The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin' is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion.
story:
At dinner, Sophia kept twirling her fork in the pasta while insisting the Eiffel Tower was in Berlin. "It's just my opinion," she said, "and my opinions are my opinions." Payton's little brother looked up from his milk like a man watching a car drive the wrong way down a one-way street.

Payton put down her spoon. She thought about the spelling bee, where she had embarrassed herself by insisting there were two r's in "harass," and how Ms. Pham had made the class look it up instead of just telling her. She had been wrong, and no amount of calling it an opinion would have added that second r. "A opinion is like, pineapple pizza is gross," she said slowly, working it out as she went. "Nobody can check that. But the Eiffel Tower is in a real place, so somebody can look it up. That makes it a claim."

"A what?"

"A claim. Like a checkable claim. It can turn out false." Payton grabbed her dad's phone from the counter, since he was being indifferent to the whole argument and only cared about his sauce. She typed EIFFEL TOWER CITY and turned the screen around.

Paris. Every single result said Paris, some of them twice, as if the internet were tired of the question.

Sophia squinted at the phone, then at her plate, then at the phone again. "Fine. So it's in Paris. But that doesn't mean I have to like it."

"That's the part that's your opinion," Payton said.

Sophia stabbed a piece of pasta and pointed her fork across the table. "Then my opinion is that the Eiffel Tower should have been in Berlin. It would look better there."

Payton slid the phone back to her dad. "You'd have to take that up with the tower."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Eyeglass prescriptions measure lens strength in diopters, with a minus sign for nearsightedness and a plus sign for farsightedness.
story:
The envelope sat on the dashboard between the front seats, and Aurora turned it over for the third time since they left the eye doctor's office. Inside was her prescription, a small card with rows of numbers. The row for her right eye said -2.00. Her left eye said -2.25.

"Minus," she said to her dad at the wheel. "My eyes got a negative score."

"They didn't fail you, sweetheart," he said, signaling for the turn onto Maple Street. "The doctor said you'd see fine once the glasses come."

Aurora slid the card back out anyway. The minus sign bothered her the way a pebble in a shoe bothered a foot, small but impossible to ignore. She remembered her grandmother's reading glasses, and how Carly's little brother had to sit at the front of the classroom because he couldn't see the board. Carly's brother got glasses last year. Aurora pulled out her phone and texted: did your brother get a minus or a plus on his prescription?

The answer came at the next red light. minus. he can't see far stuff. thats why he sits up front.

Aurora stared at the screen. She couldn't see far stuff either. That was the whole reason for today's appointment; the whiteboard had gone fuzzy from the back row, and last week she'd mistaken a dove for a pigeon and argued about it with James until the teacher settled it. So a minus meant not seeing far. She texted again: what about your mom's reading glasses?

plus, Carly wrote. plus 1.50. she can see far fine but needs help close up.

The light turned green, and the car moved forward through the intersection. Aurora held the card up beside the phone screen, comparing the two pieces of paper in her mind. Carly's brother: minus, trouble with distance. Carly's mom: plus, trouble with close things. Her own card: minus, blurry whiteboard. The pattern revolved around one simple pivot, the sign. A minus went one way, a plus went the other, and the numbers behind the sign measured how strong the lens had to be. Hers was two, which sounded like a lot until she remembered that Carly's mom's was 1.50 and nobody panicked about that.

"Dad," she said, "it's not a score at all. The minus just tells them which way my eyes need help. Far away. Carly's mom has a plus because hers need help up close."

"Huh," her dad said, glancing at her in the mirror. "So it's like directions on a map."

"Sort of." Aurora put the card back in the envelope, then took it out again and folded it carefully into the front pocket of her backpack, next to the flyer for the science fair that Mr. Lee had handed out in class. Mr. Lee had called the fair prestigious, which was why half the school wanted in, and Aurora suddenly thought she might enter. A project about how eyes and lenses work, with charts and everything.

"When the glasses come in," she said, "can we drive to the lake? I want to see the far shore."

Her dad smiled. "First stop," he said, and pointed the car toward home.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food such as milk should not sit out for more than two hours, or one hour above 32 degrees Celsius.
story:
Olivia counted the coins for the fifth time on Ms. Nakamura's garage workbench. Ms. Nakamura had spread out a jumble of change from an old coffee tin, and Olivia's job was to distinguish the quarters from everything else, fast, the way a cashier would.

"Three seventy-five for the milk," Olivia said, "so I hand over a five and I should get one dollar and twenty-five cents back."

"Exactly," said Ms. Nakamura. "Counting change is just currency math with your hands." She checked her watch. "Store opens at nine. You leave at nine sharp, and you're on your own."

Olivia's stomach did a small flip, but she slid the coins into the front pocket of the canvas bag anyway. On the garage door, taped at eye level, was a note in her mother's handwriting: "One carton of milk. Straight there, straight back. Love, Mom." Olivia read it twice, then folded it into her pocket like a lucky ticket.

The walk was easy until she passed Rania's house and Rania waved from the porch. "Come see my new bike!" It was a spontaneous invitation, and Olivia couldn't resist. She followed Rania inside, set the bag by the door, and admired the blue paint and the little bell for what felt like a few minutes. When she stepped back outside, the bag felt warm. The milk was warm. The sun was already high and the day was blazing, and suddenly she remembered something her mother had said last summer: perishable food like milk should not sit out more than two hours, or even one hour on a day above thirty-two degrees Celsius. Today was definitely one of those days.

Olivia tested the carton with her palm. Warm, but was it more than an hour warm? She couldn't see time, so she made a rule of her own: she would count backwards. The walk to the store had taken ten minutes, the walk here five, and she guessed she had been inside admiring the bike for about twenty. That was well under an hour, so the milk was probably fine, but there was no guessing twice. She said a quick goodbye to Rania and speed-walked the whole way home, carton hugged against her chest.

At the door, her mother opened it before Olivia could even knock. "Cold enough?" her mother asked, pressing the carton. "Nice and cool. Good girl." Olivia pulled out the crumpled note and the counted change, one dollar and twenty-five cents exactly, and laid them on the counter one coin at a time.

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
knowledge_domain: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
fact: Telling an anxious friend to 'just calm down' rarely helps; listening without judging and taking their worry seriously usually helps more.
story:
The kitchen smelled like butter and cinnamon when Mehtab burst through the back door, phone gripped in both hands. "The science fair is tomorrow and my display board is still at my grandma's house, two hours away, and my notes are in the bag, all of them, and I'm going to fail, Payton, I'm actually going to fail."

"Just calm down," Payton said, sliding a mug of cocoa across the counter. "It's fine. Freaking out won't fix anything."

Mehtab's face went blotchy red, and the mug sat untouched. "That's easy for you to say. You don't even understand. Forget it." She turned toward the door, and Payton's stomach dropped. She had said the wrong thing, the exactly wrong thing, and now Mehtab was leaving with the problem still wrapped around her like a backpack full of rocks.

"Wait." Payton hopped off her stool and planted herself in the doorway. "Okay, tell me the whole thing. From the start. I'm listening, I promise." Mehtab talked, and Payton did not interrupt, did not fix, did not summarize it into something small. She only nodded and asked what worried her most. The mug got picked up. The blotches faded. When Mehtab finally exhaled, Payton said, "So the real problem is the notes, not the board. A new board is feasible; my mom has poster board in the closet."

Mehtab blinked. "I was so panicked I forgot your mom is basically a craft store."

"There's one more thing," Payton said, already dialing. "Ms. Morningstar next door judges science fairs, and she told me once that teachers can help if they know early. Telling her isn't cheating, it's like, the opposite." Bias had made Mehtab sure that admitting trouble meant failure, and Payton could see that idea crumbling in real time.

Ms. Morningstar answered on the second ring, and Payton held the phone between them so Mehtab could hear her say, "Bring the board over when it's ready, dear. I'll leave the porch light on."

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: A passphrase of several random words, like the 2011 xkcd comic's example 'correct horse battery staple', is long enough to be hard to guess yet easy to remember.
story:
Brayden sat at the spare desk beside his mom's, eating the granola bar he'd been trying to consume quietly all morning. Take Your Kid to Work Day was not going well. His mom did data analysis for an insurance company, which meant she stared at spreadsheets while he stared at the wall, and the office Wi-Fi needed a password before he could do anything interesting at all.

"You can use the guest network," his mom said. "But you have to set up an account first. Use something strong, not that turtle thing."

Brayden froze. The turtle thing. Last summer he had used the same password, Turtle22, for everything: his game account, his library card, the app where he built Lego designs. Then someone got into the Lego app, sent weird messages to Karson, and Brayden spent a whole weekend changing passwords on six different sites because he'd never made them different in the first place. Karson still called him Turtle Boy sometimes, which was funny and also not.

He tried Turtle22 on the guest network anyway. The screen flashed: too common. He tried Turtle223. Too short. He sat back, chewing the last of the granola bar, and wondered why short passwords failed even when nobody could watch him type them. It was like a lock you couldn't see. Then he thought about Karlee's rubber band ball, the fat elastic one she kept in her pencil case. If you stretched a short password, it was still just one little band. But what if he stacked a bunch of words together?

Ms. Pelletier from IT walked by with a stack of keyboards. "Stuck on the password screen?" she asked. "I like a passphrase. The famous example is correct horse battery staple. Four random words, easy to remember, hard to guess." She kept walking, and Brayden stared after her because that was the silliest password he had ever heard, which meant nobody on Earth would ever guess it.

He thought of four random things he could picture: purple kangaroo trombone puddle. He typed it in, picturing a purple kangaroo playing a trombone while standing in a puddle, and laughed out loud. His mom glanced over. The screen said: password accepted.

"Purple kangaroo trombone puddle," Brayden said to no one in particular. "Don't forget it."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: In a food chain diagram, the arrows point from the thing that is eaten to the thing that eats it, showing the direction the energy flows.
story:
Rebecca crouched on the nature trail with her sketchbook, drawing a poster for Mr. Van Dijk's science class. Sun, grass, grasshopper, rabbit, fox. The trail smelled like wet leaves, and somewhere a woodpecker was attacking a tree like it owed the tree money.

Rayyan and Judy found her on the log by the creek. Rayyan held up his own poster, done in marker, arrows marching proudly down the page. "Finished. Mr. Van Dijk is going to frame it."

Judy squinted at it. "Why does it look like the grass is eating the rabbit?"

Rebecca leaned in. Every arrow pointed the wrong way, from the eater to the eaten. In Rayyan's version, the fox fed the rabbit, the rabbit fed the grasshopper, and the sun sat at the bottom like a snack.

"They're arrows," Rayyan said. "Arrows point down. Everyone knows that."

"Arrows show where the energy goes," Rebecca said slowly, mostly to herself. She flipped to her own page, which had the same problem. She had copied Rayyan's layout without thinking. She traced one with her pencil, starting at the grass. "The arrow should point from the thing that's eaten to the thing that eats it. So the energy flows up. Grass to grasshopper, grasshopper to rabbit, rabbit to fox."

"So my fox is eating sunlight," Rayyan said. "My fox is basically a plant."

Judy plucked a blade of grass and fed it to an imaginary rabbit, hand moving upward, like a tiny escalator of energy. Rebecca laughed and erased her arrows, redrawing each one pointing the other way.

"Wait," she said, staring at the chain. "What if the rabbits all disappeared?" She covered the rabbit with her thumb. The grasshoppers would multiply, the grass would get chewed to nothing, and the fox would go hungry. One missing organism and the whole page fell apart, even though you couldn't watch it happen in real time, not like watching a woodpecker.

"My poster has a chronic arrow problem," Rayyan announced. "Backward in every grade since third."

Mr. Van Dijk came down the trail with his thermos, glanced over Rebecca's shoulder, and nodded at the redone arrows. "Energy flowing uphill. Good."

Rebecca held up her thumb, still covering the rabbit. "Now watch the grasshoppers take over."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: In farsightedness, light focuses behind the retina, so near objects look blurry, and it is corrected with convex lenses.
story:
The nurse's office smelled like bandages and orange juice, and Rebecca could not stop bouncing her sneakers against the chair leg. On the counter sat a tray of trial lenses in a neutral gray case, and Mr. Novák, the school nurse, was flipping through them one by one.

"Farsightedness," he said, holding up a lens that curved outward like a tiny glass bowl. "Light focuses behind the retina instead of on it, so near objects look blurry. A convex lens like this fixes it." He slid it into the trial frame and pointed at the eye chart she had to hold close to her face. "Read the smallest line."

Rebecca read it perfectly, and she laughed out loud because the words on the poster on the far wall had gone completely fuzzy, which meant the lens was doing something real. Then Anabelle burst through the door, waving a form. "Rebecca! The art teacher wants to appoint you to the mural committee! It's a big deal, like a scholarship for painters, only with paint instead of money!" Anabelle's own glasses had thick lenses, and Rebecca had always noticed they made Anabelle's eyes look bigger, like a friendly owl.

Rebecca frowned at her reflection in the little mirror. Her trial lens made her eye look bigger too, exactly like Anabelle's. That was odd. Marcel wore glasses, and his eyes always looked smaller, like buttons. So the lenses must be different. Marcel said things far away were blurry for him; she was the opposite, blurry up close. She grabbed a pen and held it at arm's length, then pulled it slowly toward her nose. Blurry at the far end, sharp up close. Her eyes were the opposite of Marcel's, so her lens had to be the opposite of his. It was like a rule, and she had just tested it herself.

"Mr. Novák," she said, "does a lens like mine make eyes look bigger because it's convex, fixing farsightedness where light focuses behind the retina, while Marcel's does the opposite?"

"Exactly right," he said, scribbling her prescription.

Then Anabelle leaned close to the mirror, squinted, and pointed at the tray. "Hey, those trial lenses in the gray case. My glasses fell in the pond at recess. Can I try some?"

Mr. Novák picked up a convex lens, held it up to Anabelle's chart, and raised his eyebrows. "Anabelle, you just read that tiny line better than with your own glasses. Want to sit in the chair?"

Rebecca jumped up. "I'll trade you turns on the mural brainstorm if you let me pick your frames."

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Snow looks white because its many clear ice crystals scatter and reflect all colors of light in every direction.
story:
Nathan pressed his nose against the kitchen window and could not believe his luck. School was canceled, the whole street was buried, and he was free until dinner. Then he noticed something odd that stuck in his mind like a splinter. The icicles hanging from the gutters were clear as glass, so clear he could see the fence through them. But the yard underneath was blinding white. Same stuff, ice and ice. "How does clear ice make a white yard?" he asked his dad, who only shrugged and said something about shoveling later.

Nathan pulled on his boots and tromped next door, where Jaycob and Alexy were already building a fort at Ms. Marino's place. She had told the boys they could play in her yard as long as they stayed off her porch, because the old cushions stored there were flammable and she did not want anyone fooling with her space heater. Nathan felt a flicker of resentment about that rule, since her porch had the best sledding ramp, but he pushed it aside. He had bigger things on his mind.

"Look," he said, holding up an icicle he had snapped off the fence. He held it beside a handful of snow. "This is clear. This is white. It's the same water." Alexy squinted. "Maybe the icicle is just special." Nathan crushed the snow in his fist until it packed into a ball, then scraped a thin shaving off the icicle with his mitten. The shaving was clear too. So it wasn't the ice itself. He looked closely at the snow on his glove, and there it was: tiny separate crystals, dozens of them, each one sparkling like a bit of glass. One crystal alone was clear, but a whole pile of them had to be different.

"I get it," Nathan said, waving the icicle like a pointer. "Snow is millions of clear ice crystals, and all those crystals scatter and reflect every color of light in every direction. All the colors bouncing everywhere, all at once." Jaycob grabbed a handful and tilted it toward the sun. "So one piece is clear, but a bunch of them together looks white." Alexy threw her arms wide. "Then let's make the biggest bunch ever!" She patted a block onto the fort wall, and Nathan ran for another armload of snow.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Psychologist John Suler described the 'online disinhibition effect' in 2004: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face.
story:
The bus smelled of wet raincoats, and Muhammad was halfway through a video on his phone when Bo leaned over the seat. "Look at this," Bo said, holding up his own screen. It was a comment under Alexane's art post, the one of the fox she had drawn for the science fair. The comment said her fox looked like roadkill, and it came from a boy in their class named in the username but unmistakable anyway. "That's Devon," Muhammad said slowly. "Devon held the door for her yesterday." Bo shrugged. "People are weird online."

Muhammad could not stop thinking about it. Devon had never once been rude in person, not even when Mr. Okafor made them all run laps in the rain. In class he said please and thank you like the words cost him nothing. But online he wrote things that would make a substitute teacher cry. It was like two different Devons, and Muhammad wanted to know which one was real. That evening he typed the strange pattern into the school laptop: people say mean things online but not face to face. The first result was an article about a psychologist, John Suler, who had described the "online disinhibition effect" back in 2004. Muhammad read the words twice. So it was a thing people had actually studied, a thing with a name. It did not make Devon's comment okay. But it meant Devon was probably not a secret monster, just a regular person who let his worst self out when nobody could see his face.

The next morning Muhammad found Alexane at her locker. She was stuffing her sketchbook into her bag like she wanted to bury it. "You saw it," she said, not asking. "Everyone saw it." Muhammad hesitated, then said, "I read something. In 2004 a psychologist named John Suler described it. He called it the online disinhibition effect. People say things online that they'd hold back from saying face to face." Alexane frowned. "So that makes it fine?" "No," Muhammad said. "It makes it a pattern instead of a you problem. There's a difference."

At lunch, Devon's usual table had an empty seat, and Devon was eating alone near the recycling bins, eyes fixed on his tray. Muhammad had planned to stay angry. Instead he carried his tray over and sat down. "Your comment on Alexane's fox," he said. "She almost quit drawing over it." Devon's ears went red. "It was supposed to be a joke," he mumbled. "It wasn't," Muhammad said. "Show her your face, not your username." Devon pushed his food around for a long moment, then stood up, and Muhammad watched him walk across the cafeteria toward Alexane's table with the comment still open on his phone, thumb hovering over the delete button.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Wet oven mitts can burn your hands, because water in the cloth carries heat quickly and can turn to steam.
story:
Connor had never baked anything alone before, and the recipe on the counter made it sound both easy and mysterious. Preheat the oven. Mix the dry. Fold in the wet. He wondered what "fold" really meant, and whether it mattered if he just stirred. His friend Kellen sat on the counter stool, reading the recipe over his shoulder and tapping the line that said chopped walnuts.

"We can't use those," Kellen said. "My little sister has a walnut allergy. One bite and she swells up." So they swapped in blueberries, and Connor carefully measured the flour, leveling the cup with the back of a knife like his mom did. He turned the dial on the oven and watched the numbers climb. Why did the oven have to be hot before the muffins even went in? He decided it must be like warming up before a race, so the batter got the same treatment from the first second.

The first splash happened at the sink. Connor rinsed the measuring cup, and water spattered across the oven mitt hanging on the hook beside him, soaking one corner dark. He didn't notice. Twenty-two minutes later, the timer beeped, and he pulled the mitt onto his hand and reached for the oven door.

"Stop!" Kellen grabbed his wrist. "It's wet. Wet oven mitts can burn your hands. The water in the cloth carries heat fast, and it can turn to steam."

Connor stared at the damp patch. He had assumed a mitt was a mitt, wet or dry, but if the water in the cloth carried heat quickly, then the wet part was almost like no protection at all. He tested the idea instead of arguing. He ran more water over the mitt's corner, hung it on the hook, and found the dry one in the drawer, sliding his hand in and lifting the muffin tray out smooth and steady. The tops were golden and domed, and he counted twelve perfect little crowns.

"They look like something from one of those prestigious baking shows," Kellen said, already reaching for one. Connor dodged him with the tray. "Not yet. We let them cool, and the first one is mine." Kellen tried to evade him around the island, snatching at a blueberry that had tumbled onto the counter, and Connor stood guard over the tray until the smell of warm blueberries filled the whole kitchen.

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these versions are called isotopes, such as carbon-12 with 6 neutrons and carbon-14 with 8.
story:
Aurora spread the materials across the kitchen table: a bag of red marbles, a bag of blue ones, and a spool of thin wire for the orbits. The science project was due tomorrow morning, and Mr. Jean-Louis had been clear that the model atom had to have every particle in the right place. Six red marbles for protons, she reminded herself, going in the nucleus at the center. The blue marbles were the neutrons, and the small silver beads strung on wire loops would be the electrons. She was halfway through gluing the nucleus when Katelyn and Kyla arrived with their own boxes, because the three of them had planned to finish together before dinner.

Katelyn dumped her supplies out and frowned at Aurora's model. "You put eight blue marbles in the middle. I only have six. One of us is wrong."

"They can't both be carbon then," Kyla said, picking up a blue marble and turning it over. "If the neutrons are different, it's a different thing, right? Like, one of them isn't carbon at all."

Aurora looked from one model to the other. Katelyn's nucleus had six red and six blue; hers had six red and eight blue. She counted the electrons on both, and both models had six silver beads circling in their wire orbits. The protons matched too. Only the middle differed, and the middle was the part nobody could actually see inside a real atom. She sat back and thought about that. If the protons and electrons were the same, then maybe the neutrons were not what decided what the element was.

She fetched her science book from her backpack and flipped through the chapter until she found the page on atoms. There it was, in a small paragraph beside a lush, colorful diagram of a nucleus. She read it twice, then set the book down between the two models so they could both see.

"Listen to this," Aurora said. "Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons. Those versions are called isotopes." She pointed to the examples printed below. "Like carbon-12, which has 6 neutrons, and carbon-14, which has 8. They're both carbon."

Katelyn let out a breath and laughed. "So we're both right? All this arguing for nothing."

"That's the verdict," Kyla said, grinning. "Both carbon, just different isotopes."

Aurora decided to incorporate both versions into the project. She glued a small label to her model that read carbon-14 and helped Katelyn letter carbon-12 on hers, then wired the silver electrons into two neat loops so the orbits would not sag. They worked while the kitchen filled with the smell of dinner, checking each other's glue and trading marbles until every particle sat where it belonged.

When they were done, Aurora carried both atoms to the window ledge, where the late sun caught the wire orbits and made them shine. Katelyn nudged her and pointed at the two models side by side.

"Same element, different middle," Katelyn said. "Mr. Jean-Louis is going to love this."

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: Transition words such as first, however, furthermore and therefore link paragraphs and show the reader how one idea relates to the next.
story:
Emma had written three paragraphs about why the school should have a longer lunch period, and every sentence felt like a separate stone dropped on the desk. She read the pages again at the corner table in the library, near the window where afternoon light came through the glass and threw a small prism of colour across her notebook. "It's all here," she muttered. "But it sounds like a robot wrote it."

Tegan slid into the chair across from her and picked up the draft. She read the first paragraph, then the second, her finger tracing each line. "The ideas are good. They're just not connected. It's like the paragraphs are strangers standing in a line." Emma frowned and laid the pages side by side. Her first point was that students were hungry. Her second point was that rushing caused stomachaches. Her third point was that better lunch breaks would probably improve afternoon classes. They were related, she could see that now, but nothing on the page told the reader how.

She borrowed a green pen from Tegan and began to test a simple idea: what if one word at each seam could carry the reader across? Before her first point she wrote "First," and the sentence seemed to stand up straighter. Between hunger and stomachaches she wrote "However," because the second idea pushed back against the first. Before her third point she added "Furthermore," and at the end, before her final sentence, she wrote "Therefore." She read the whole essay out loud in a low voice, and the paragraphs that had been strangers now walked in step, each word a small push that seemed to propel the reader forward.

Mr. Nkosi passed by on his way to the returns cart and paused. "That sounded smooth," he said. "What changed?" Emma held up the draft, green words standing out along the margins. "Transition words," she said. "First, however, furthermore, therefore. They link the paragraphs and show how one idea relates to the next." He nodded and moved on, and Emma flattened the pages on the table, sunlight striping across the green ink. "Okay," she said to Tegan. "Read it one more time, but pretend you're the principal."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: A boundary is a limit a person sets about what they are comfortable with, such as how others treat them, touch them or use their belongings.
story:
Aria pushed her pasta around the plate while her dad unfolded a brochure about the old garage. He wanted to renovate it into a workshop, and he had talked about nothing else for a week. "This spring," he said, tapping the page. "I already priced the lumber." Her mom sprinkled cheese on her own plate and studied Aria's face. "You've been quiet since you got home. Trouble at school?"

Aria put down her fork. "Marcus read my phone today." She made herself keep going. "I went to get water, and when I came back he was scrolling through my messages. He laughed at one, from Aidan, and I felt my whole chest go hot." Her mom asked what she had done, and Aria described how she had grabbed the phone and stormed to the other side of the room, and how Marcus had followed her around all afternoon asking what was wrong. "Every time he came near, my stomach knotted up. I couldn't even do my science homework, the ecosystem project that's due Friday. I just sat there drawing the same pond three times."

"Did you tell him why you were upset?" her dad asked. Aria shook her head. Her mom said, "He can't fix what he doesn't know he broke." That sentence stuck in Aria's head like a splinter. She thought about the morning, before any of it happened, when Marcus had begged to see the new game on her phone and she had said no, and he had picked it up anyway while she was tying her shoe. He had done the same thing last month with her sketchbook. It was a pattern, and the pattern had a cause she had never named out loud. She had never once told him where her lines were.

"Mr. Morningstar says a boundary is a limit you set about what you're comfortable with," Aria said slowly, remembering the poster outside the counselor's office. "Like how people treat you, touch you, or use your stuff." She looked up. "I never actually set one with Marcus. I just got mad." Her dad slid the flammable label on the paint thinner out of the way so he could see her across the table. "So set it. Tomorrow."

The next day Aria found Marcus at his locker. "I'm not mad forever," she said, "but here's my boundary: you don't pick up my phone, my sketchbook, anything of mine, unless I say yes. That's the rule from now on." Marcus blinked, then hung his head. "I only did it because you never let me in," he mumbled. "Aidan gets to see everything." Aria hadn't thought of that. "Then ask, and I'll show you things. Ask, every time." Marcus stuck out his hand, and she shook it, feeling the knot in her stomach finally loosen.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because the phrase 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death.
story:
The cultural festival smelled like grilled lamb, fried dough and something sweet Dylan couldn't name, and he loved it already. He raced past the craft tables with Inara and Anna-Eve, but really he was on a mission. His neighbor Mr. Marino's colleague, a Chinese family who had just moved in down the street, had invited everyone to their housewarming tomorrow, and Dylan had exactly one afternoon to find the perfect gift before the festival's gift stalls closed at four.

"There!" Anna-Eve pointed at a booth stacked with handmade clocks, each one painted with tiny cranes. "Every housewarming needs a clock." It was beautiful, dark red with a brass pendulum, and the price was right. Dylan pulled out his money, and the vendor smiled and reached for a box.

Then he noticed the vendor's smile flicker. She glanced at the clock, then at Dylan, and hesitated with the box halfway across the counter. Dylan had learned to notice hesitations; his little cousin was never immune to being caught mid-mischief, and that same guilty pause was written on the vendor's face now. Why would she hesitate to sell her own product? He slowed down and asked, "Is something wrong with it? Does it not keep time?"

She lowered the box. "Nothing is wrong with it," she said. "But you are buying a gift for a Chinese family, yes? I heard you. In Chinese, giving a clock sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death." She said it gently, like a warning about stepping on a loose board.

Dylan put his money back in his pocket so fast he nearly dropped the quarters. That explained the flicker, and probably a dozen other stalls too: at the tea booth, at the scarf table, people kept steering customers toward some gifts and away from others, following rules he couldn't see. So he decided to test it. He walked back to the clock booth and asked, loudly enough for the crowd, "So a clock is a bad gift for a Chinese household?" Three separate vendors nodded at once. One held up a teapot instead. Confirmed, Dylan thought, feeling like a detective closing a case.

He didn't have time to mope, because Inara was already dragging him toward a booth of lacquered tea sets that would generate jealous gasps from his whole class. He picked one painted with fish, paid, and hugged the box the rest of the afternoon while Anna-Eve bought dumplings that steamed in the cold air and Inara won a paper lantern that glowed orange against the gray sky.

The next evening at the housewarming, Dylan presented the tea set with both hands, the way he'd watched the vendor demonstrate. The grandmother of the family took it, beamed, and immediately poured him tea, insisting he hold the tiny cup with two fingers and drain it in exactly three sips. "In our house, one sip is rude and four is greedy," she teased. Dylan raised his cup and said, "Three sips it is," and the whole kitchen burst out laughing just as the kettle whistled.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word diaspora comes from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors.
story:
Cole had been trying to evade Mattea's little brother all afternoon, but the boy kept appearing at the kitchen table where Cole and Mattea were painting a banner for Saturday's cultural festival at the community centre. Mattea's family was from Trinidad by way of Nova Scotia, and her grandmother had asked for a banner with the word diaspora painted in tall gold letters. Neither of them knew what it meant, and that was the problem. Mattea's grandmother had gone to the shop for more paint, and the festival would look strange if the banner carried a word nobody at the table could explain.

"Maybe it's a kind of drum," Mattea said, tilting her head at the letters.

Cole thought about that. He traced the shape of the word with his finger in the air. It didn't sound like a drum. It sounded like something old, something with a story behind it, the way words in Mr. Charles's class sometimes did. "It has 'spora' in it," he said. "Like spores. The things that float off mushrooms and land far away." He had a theory forming: maybe the word was about things that scattered. He grabbed the paper towel he'd been using as a coaster and started listing everything he knew about Mattea's family. Her grandmother grew up in Nova Scotia. Her great-great-grandparents had come there from somewhere else. The family had cousins in Toronto, London and Brooklyn, and they all sent cards at Christmas.

"So the family got spread out," Mattea said slowly, following his finger across the napkin map he was sketching. "Far from wherever it started." Her brother, still lurking by the fridge, finally spoke up. "Nana says that word all the time on the phone. She says, 'We are a diaspora people.'" He said it in a wobbly imitation of the grandmother's voice that made even Cole laugh.

When her grandmother returned, she set down the paint tins and looked at the banner. Cole asked, straight out, whether diaspora meant scattered, like spores from a mushroom. Her grandmother's face opened into a smile that made her eyes vanish. "The word comes from a Greek word meaning scattering," she said. "And it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors." She said it plainly, the way she might name a recipe, then touched the gold letters with one finger.

"It's like the word was waiting for us to figure it out," Cole said. Mattea's grandmother chuckled and said the afternoon had not been wasted leisure after all. Mattea's brother, who had been quietly hoping someone would ask him to help all day, held up a paintbrush and asked if he could do the sparkly border, since his painting was exceptional for a seven-year-old. Mattea looked at Cole, and Cole nodded. They let him do it, and when he dropped a blot of gold on the word itself, nobody minded, because from across the kitchen it looked exactly like a scattered star.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power, and a half-full one for about 24 hours, if the door stays closed.
story:
Joseph lay on the couch with a candle flickering on the coffee table, listening to the rain hammer the roof. The whole street had gone dark at seven o'clock, and the power company's recording, which his dad had called twice, would only say that crews were working to generate electricity again as fast as they could. Joseph thought that phrase was funny, as if the storm had stolen the electricity and the crews had to generate a fresh batch.

"Alright," his dad said, pacing the living room with a flashlight under his chin so he looked like a jack-o'-lantern. "The big question is the freezer. If everything in there thaws, we're eating chili for a week."

"We could invite Bella and Isaac over for a chili festival," Joseph said. "Bring your own spoon."

His dad laughed, then stopped. "Seriously, though. How long do we have?"

Joseph sat up. He remembered something his science tutor had mentioned last month, an offhand comment during a lesson Joseph had mostly spent doodling. Something about freezers and outages. He closed his eyes and pulled it back. A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power. A half-full one, only about 24, if the door stays closed. That part mattered: the door stays closed. The cold wasn't magic; it was a supply, like money in a piggy bank, and every open door spent some.

"Twenty-four hours," he said, opening his eyes. "Maybe. But only if nobody opens it."

"Why twenty-four?"

"Because it's only half full. Remember, we ate all the migratory birds, I mean the chicken, last week. Turkey week, you called it." Joseph was fairly sure chickens weren't migratory, but his dad had been calling it that for days and it had stuck. "A full one would last about 48 hours. That's what my tutor said. Half full, half the time, roughly. So we need power back by tomorrow night, or we start cooking."

His dad shone the flashlight into the freezer, careful to open the door only a crack and only once. Bags of peas, two pizzas, a lonely box of popsicles. Half full, confirmed.

"Twenty-four hours," his dad repeated. "Okay. New rule. Nobody breathes on this freezer."

"I breathe very cold air anyway," Joseph said. "It's my superpower."

At nine the next morning, Joseph stood at the window watching the rain lighten up. The street was still dark. He did the math again. Seven o'clock last night plus twenty-four hours was seven o'clock tonight. Plenty of margin, as long as the door stayed shut, but the clock was real now, ticking quietly in a sealed white box in the kitchen.

At noon the lights blinked on, and the fridge hummed like it had never been away. Joseph ran to the kitchen, held his hand near the freezer, and didn't open it.

"Dad!" he shouted. "Victory dance in the living room. Bring the popsicles."

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
knowledge_domain: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
fact: Anxiety triggers the body's fight-or-flight response, releasing adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and breathing even when there is no real danger.
story:
Scarlett had been looking forward to the camp talent show all week, but on the night before it, Alexis wasn't acting like herself. At dinner she barely touched her pasta, and when Scarlett asked her to run lines for their comedy skit, Alexis's words came out fast and shallow, like she had just sprinted up the hill to the mess hall.

"Are you okay?" Scarlett asked.

"Fine," Alexis said. "I just can't get my breath right. And my heart is doing this weird pounding thing, like my body thinks I'm in actual danger. From a skit." She laughed, but it was a thin sound.

Scarlett had felt something like that herself once, before a spelling bee, and she had read about it in a book her aunt lent her. When anxiety kicks in, the body switches to fight-or-flight and releases adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and breathing even when there is no real danger at all. So Alexis's pounding heart didn't mean she was sick. It meant she was scared, even though Alexis kept insisting she was fine.

But telling wasn't the whole answer, and Scarlett knew it. If she marched Alexis straight to Mr. Novák, Alexis might resign from the skit just to make the feeling stop. Scarlett had a bias toward fixing things herself, but she wasn't a counselor, and she might get it wrong. So she tested a smaller idea. She sat with Alexis by the lake and breathed slowly, in for four, out for four, until Alexis's breathing matched hers.

It helped, but not enough. Alexis's hands were still trembling. So Scarlett walked with her to find Mr. Novák, who turned out to be quietly competent at exactly this. He moved their skit to the middle of the show, gave Alexis a spot near the back curtain, and told her she could step out any time.

The next evening, Alexis stood in the wings with her heart hammering, and she knew exactly why. She walked on anyway, and the first laugh from the crowd came faster than her pulse.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Research on children at overnight camps has found that most campers feel at least some homesickness during their stay, and for most of them it stays mild.
story:
Colton set his tray down at the end of the long table and stared at his macaroni. Four days at Camp Windrow, and tonight was the campfire and the talent show, and everyone in his cabin acted like the whole thing was wonderful. Mavrick was already planning a comedy act. Miriam from Cabin 4 had been practicing a song all week. Colton had signed up for nothing, because every night, when the lights went out, his chest got tight and he thought about his dog, Biscuit, sleeping on the kitchen floor at home.

He was sure he was the only one. Nobody else said anything about it. At breakfast they laughed about the swim test. At lunch they argued about hockey. Colton kept his mouth shut and figured there was something wrong with him.

That evening, before dinner, Mr. Mensah, the camp director, stood at the front of the dining hall and held up a clipboard. "Quick announcement. A few years back, researchers studied kids at overnight camps, and they found that most campers feel at least some homesickness during their stay. For most of them, it stays mild." He tapped the clipboard. "So if that's you, you're in the majority. Now, meatloaf is served."

Colton sat very still. Most campers. He looked down the table at Mavrick, who was stacking crackers into a tower, and tested an idea. "Mavrick," he said, "do you ever miss home? Like at night?"

Mavrick's tower wobbled. "Every single night," Mavrick said. "I keep a photo of my cat in my pillowcase. Don't tell anyone."

Miriam leaned over from the next table. "I cried on Tuesday. During hygiene hour, when everyone was brushing teeth. I figured nobody would notice with all the water running."

Colton laughed, and it came out louder than he meant to. The whole table turned, and a kid from Cabin 6 named nobody said, "Wait, you guys get homesick too?" and then six kids were talking at once. Colton felt like he'd solved a mystery. The problem hadn't been inside him. It had been a rule nobody said out loud, and now that it was said, it seemed smaller.

"Then it's probable our whole cabin feels it," Colton said. "So here's my idea. We all go to the talent show tonight, and we do an act together. We go up and just tell them. Every kid in this hall who misses home, stand up."

Mr. Mensah was passing with a pitcher of water. "That's an act I'd pay to see," he said.

The campfire crackled, and when Colton's cabin was called, Mavrick walked up first, and Colton followed. "How many of you miss home at night?" Mavrick asked the crowd. "Be honest." Hands went up all over the benches, more than Colton could count, and Miriam stood up in the second row and started to sing.

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Frying an egg is a chemical change, because heat permanently changes the proteins in the egg white so it turns solid and white.
story:
The mystery on Mr. Halvorsen's desk was two plates, and Hazel couldn't stop staring at them. On the left sat a mound of shredded cheese, already softened back into a puddle. On the right sat something that looked like scrambled egg, cold and rubbery now. "One of these went through a physical change," Mr. Halvorsen said, tapping the desk, "and one went through a chemical change. By Friday, you tell me which is which, and prove it."

Hazel wanted the answer more than she wanted recess. Dania wanted something else entirely: she needed Friday's point, because her average in science had slipped and her mother had threatened to confiscate her tablet until it climbed. "If we work together, we both get the point," Dania argued as they walked to the cafeteria. Kaia trailed behind them, crunching an apple. "You could just say the cheese melted and melted means physical," Kaia offered. "But then the egg is chemical by default, and I don't like guessing by default," Hazel said. "I like proving it." Dania rolled her eyes, but she scribbled both ideas in her notebook anyway.

That afternoon, Hazel dismantled her reasoning piece by piece at the lab table. Melting, she remembered, was like ice becoming water: it could go back. Physical changes were reversible. So her test had to be simple and a little gross. She borrowed a fried egg from the cafeteria line, let it cool until the bell rang, and then tried to turn the white back to clear. She poked it. She pressed it with a spatula. It stayed white and solid, the equivalent of trying to unburn a piece of toast. Something in it had been permanently changed.

"Then it's not physical," Dania whispered, watching the stubborn egg with wide eyes. "Heat permanently changes the proteins in the egg white," Hazel said quietly, mostly to herself, "so it turns solid and white, and it can't go clear again." Across the room, a boy from sixth period argued loudly that his Chromebook had caught a virus over the weekend, which was a change you couldn't undo either, but nobody listened to him.

On Friday, Mr. Halvorsen set the two plates out again and asked who had an answer. Hazel raised her hand so fast her chair squeaked. "The cheese is the physical change, because it melted and can melt back and forth," she said. "And the egg is a chemical change, because once the heat cooks the white solid and white, it's stuck that way forever." Mr. Halvorsen smiled and slid the plates toward her. "Show me," he said. Hazel picked up the cold fried egg and pressed down hard on the white with her thumb.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Quito, the capital of Ecuador, lies less than a quarter of a degree south of the equator, so its latitude is almost zero.
story:
Gabriella spread the atlas across the kitchen table and pinned the corners with two mugs and a salt shaker. Her assignment was due Monday: pick a capital city and give its exact location using latitude and longitude. Kiana had already texted that she was doing Paris, which meant half the class would probably do Paris too. Gabriella wanted something better. She traced a finger along the horizontal lines, counting degrees, then stopped. Somewhere on this map there had to be a city sitting almost on zero.

The problem was the equator itself, that bold line crossing the map like a belt, mostly over ocean. She dragged a chair closer and followed it across the Atlantic, over Brazil, past a crowd of small blue numbers. She skipped dinner once already that week, and Dad, who was between jobs since the recession shut down the plant, kept walking through to refill his coffee. She persisted anyway, running her fingertip along the printed line until it crossed the western edge of South America.

There it was. Quito, capital of Ecuador, printed in capital letters just below the equator. She checked the numbers along the sides of the map and did the math twice. Less than a quarter of a degree south of the line. Its latitude was almost zero. She leaned back and smelled the paper and dust of the old atlas.

She called Kiana. "Guess what country has a capital with a latitude that starts with zero," she said.

"Zero? That's impossible. Every place is north or south of something."

"Not Quito. It's barely south of the equator at all, less than a quarter of a degree, so the latitude is almost nothing."

Kiana was quiet for a second. "You're doing Ecuador, aren't you."

"Already written down. Longitude next." Gabriella put the phone on speaker, picked up her pencil, and turned the page toward the vertical lines.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Phishing is a scam in which someone pretends to be a trusted company or person to trick you into giving away passwords or other private information.
story:
Wyatt's new phone sat on his desk inside his math book, hidden but buzzing like a trapped bee. He had owned it for exactly one day, and he already felt the weight of the obligation his parents had laid on him: one careless mistake and the phone went back in the drawer until high school. Mr. Abdi was writing fractions on the board, so Wyatt slid the phone out half an inch and read the text that had just arrived. "WARNING: Your BlockCraft account will be deleted in 24 hours unless you verify your password now. Tap here." His stomach dropped. He had spent two whole years building his worlds.

He almost tapped the link right there. Instead he wrote a note and passed it to Rachel, who sat diagonally behind him and knew more about phones than anyone in sixth grade. "Did you get a weird text about BlockCraft?" Her answer came back folded into a tiny square. "Myra got one too. We deleted ours. Ask Mr. Abdi after class about it, he knows." Wyatt turned the problem over in his head. He tried to diagnose it like a math problem. If BlockCraft really wanted to delete accounts, why would a random text arrive on the very first day he owned a phone, before he had even told anyone his number? And Myra's text was identical. Companies didn't send the exact same message to different people and demand a password through a text. Something was pretending to be BlockCraft.

When the bell rang, he hung back. "Mr. Abdi, if a text says it's BlockCraft and asks for your password, is it real?" Mr. Abdi set down his marker. "Sounds like phishing," he said. "That's when someone pretends to be a trusted company or person to trick you into giving away passwords or other private information." Wyatt's mind flashed to his note, to Myra's identical message, and everything clicked. He deleted the text before he even left the room, then messaged Myra from the hallway, glad he still had his worlds, his number, and his phone.

knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when proteins in wheat flour mix with water, and kneading the dough makes the gluten stronger and stretchier.
story:
Jace stood in the quiet kitchen with flour on his nose and a promise to keep: dinner bread, made entirely by him, while his mom worked late. He had eaten his grandmother's bread a hundred times, but he had never actually listened to the part about kneading. He only remembered her saying something about "gluten" while her hands folded and turned the dough like she was tucking it into bed.

He mixed flour and water into a shaggy lump, then split it in two. One half he plopped into a bowl right away. The other half he pushed and folded and squashed on the counter. His arms ached after four minutes, and the dough still tore when he pulled it, like wet paper. He kept going, glancing at the clock, until ten whole minutes had passed. Then he stretched a pinch of it, and it pulled into a thin window without ripping. "So that's what you were doing, Grandma," he said to the empty room.

While he waited for the dough to rise, his friend Candice knocked on the door, drawn by the smell and by the hope of leftovers. She wanted a slice warm, with butter, and she made this known immediately. "I'll trade you my help," she offered. Jace said she could comply with house rules first: shoes off, hands washed, and no sneezing near the risen dough. She agreed, mostly because the dough had puffed up like a pillow and she wanted to poke it.

The two loaves came out of the oven an hour later, golden and thumping hollowly when tapped. The unkneaded one had risen crooked and dense, like a sad biscuit. Jace tore both open to compare. The ten-minute one stretched into soft strands; the lazy one crumbled into gravelly chunks. "It's the gluten," he told Candice, sawing a slice. "It forms when the flour proteins meet the water, and kneading makes it stronger and stretchier." Candice chewed the good bread, then nibbled the bad one, then made a face like a cat confronting a lemon.

"You turned one loaf into a science experiment," she said, reaching for the butter dish. Jace set the dense loaf aside for the birds and texted his mom a photo of the good one, with a note: Dinner solved, mortgage payment not required, just flour and water. Then he cut Candice the biggest slice, set it on a plate, and slid it across the counter like a waiter in a very tranquil little bakery. "Order up," he said, and took a bow.
